diagnostic_evidence.quote: $\kappa=0$ is always an eigenvalue for any $n$, since we may choose $v\equiv w$ to be any harmonic function on $D$

issues.failure_explanation: The paper itself shows that kappa=0 has a nontrivial (indeed infinite-dimensional) kernel, i.e. it is an eigenvalue. It therefore lies in the point spectrum, as an eigenvalue of infinite multiplicity and hence in the essential spectrum. The continuous spectrum consists of points where the operator is injective, so it is disjoint from the point spectrum. The inference from an infinite-dimensional eigenspace to continuous spectrum is invalid.

failure_location.quote: we conclude that $0$ belongs to the \emph{continuous spectrum} of the ITP

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace 'continuous spectrum' with 'point (essential) spectrum: an eigenvalue of infinite multiplicity'.
issues.overall_effect: The spectral classification of kappa=0 is mis-stated. The justification for excluding kappa=0 survives, and no formal result depends on it.
issues.title: kappa=0 is an eigenvalue, hence point spectrum, not continuous spectrum
issues.why_classification: A one-phrase correction of a side remark; no result or guarantee is affected.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Now, assume that $p\mapsto(\kappa_p,v_p,w_p)$ are all continuously differentiable at $p=p^\star$, so that the above formula holds there.
because the integral factor stays bounded as a consequence of the continuous differentiability of the eigenfunction trajectory near $p^\star$

issues.failure_explanation: The contradiction argument assumes C^1 regularity on a neighbourhood of p*, because it needs boundedness of v_p', w_p' as p->p*. It therefore only proves that the trajectory is not C^1 at p*. Mere differentiability at p* gives no bound on the derivatives near p*, so the limiting argument does not exclude it, yet the statement claims non-differentiability. cor:bifurc is said to follow by the same argument and inherits the gap.

failure_location.quote: Then $p=p^\star$ gives rise to an exceptional point, since the eigenpair trajectory is non-differentiable there.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Assume only differentiability at p*. Then (v_p,w_p) is continuous at p*, so I(p*)=lim I(p)=0 by lem:zeronorm on the non-real side. Equation (realimagkappa) at p* then gives 0 = (1/2)kappa*^2 int n'|w|^2, a contradiction. Alternatively, weaken the statement to 'not continuously differentiable'.
issues.overall_effect: The stated conclusion (non-differentiability) is stronger than what the given proof establishes (not C^1).
issues.title: Proof only excludes continuous differentiability, but the theorem asserts non-differentiability
issues.why_classification: A short local argument using quantities already in the proof restores the full claim.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Differentiating the above expression and enforcing the correct asymptotic order of $\kappa_p'$ as $p\to p^\star$ proves that $M'=M$, yielding the first claim.
Note that $M$ distinct eigenvalue trajectories must be present near an order-$M$ bifurcation
The claim follows by \cref{cor:bifurc_sufficient}, noting that $J_m'(\kappa_{p^\star})\neq0$ since nontrivial Bessel roots are simple.

issues.failure_explanation: A general Puiseux branch with cycle length M' is kappa*+sum_k c_k (p-p*)^{k/M'}, and its first nonzero coefficient may have k>1. Matching derivative orders only identifies the leading exponent, not the cycle length (the bifurcation order). Forward counterexample: kappa-kappa* = a(p-p*)^{1/2} + b(p-p*)^{3/4} gives, via eq:bifurc_ord, I=(p-p*)^{1/2} times a continuous nonzero factor, so M=2 in the hypothesis, yet the cycle has 4 branches. Converse counterexample: the cubic cycle (kappa-kappa*)^3=(p-p*)^2 has a real branch on both sides with kappa' ~ (p-p*)^{-1/3}. Then I ~ (p-p*)^{1/3} and I ~ (kappa-kappa*)^{1/2}, not the claimed (p-p*)^{2/3} and (kappa-kappa*)^2.

failure_location.quote: Namely, a \emph{Puiseux series} for $\kappa_p$ must exist: for some $M'\in\{2,3,\ldots\}$, and $c\in\mathbb{C}_{\neq0}$,

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Either add the hypothesis that the leading Puiseux exponent equals 1/(cycle length), or restate the theorem in terms of the leading exponent: the forward direction then yields a bifurcation whose order is a multiple of M, and the converse relates the root order of I to the leading exponent k/M. Recover cubicity on the disk by citing thm:old.
issues.overall_effect: Neither direction of the order characterization is proved. Only the leading exponent 1/M is established. The 'cubic' conclusion of prop:disk:bifurc, derived from it, is likewise unproved.
issues.title: Bifurcation-order identification assumes a nonzero first Puiseux coefficient
issues.why_classification: A contained extra hypothesis or a limited weakening of a main theorem is needed, and the disk cubicity claim must be re-sourced; the results remain recognizably comparable.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Consider an eigenpair trajectory as in \cref{prop:annulus:bifurc}
(by expanding the square and exploiting the realness of Bessel functions for real inputs)

issues.failure_explanation: The proof changes variables x=kappa*rho and applies eq:integral_sum, which needs real x (real Bessel values), so it requires kappa_p real. For non-real kappa_p, lem:zeronorm gives I=0 and hence Ibar=0. The right-hand side does not vanish in general: its r->0 (disk) analogue is |J_m(kappa)|^2>0 for non-real kappa. The proposition nevertheless covers any trajectory as in prop:annulus:bifurc.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add the hypothesis kappa_p in R (Ibar=0 otherwise by lem:zeronorm), as is done for the disk formula.
issues.overall_effect: As stated, the formula is false on non-real portions of trajectories. Its intended use on real trajectories is unaffected.
issues.title: Annulus indicator formula stated for all trajectories but valid only for real eigenvalues
issues.why_classification: Adding a standard local hypothesis preserves every intended use and conclusion.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: undergoes bifurcation if and only if $\|v_p\|_{L^\infty(\partial B_1)}=r\|v_p\|_{L^\infty(\partial B_r)}$

issues.failure_explanation: For v=c(rho)phi(m theta), arc length gives ||v||^2_{L^2(dB_1)} = a_m pi |c(1)|^2 and ||v||^2_{L^2(dB_r)} = r a_m pi |c(r)|^2. So |c(1)|=r|c(r)| is equivalent to ||v||_{L^2(dB_1)} = sqrt(r) ||v||_{L^2(dB_r)}, not to equality of the norms; with the measure d theta it would be a factor r. The stated equivalence is false for 0<r<1.

failure_location.quote: this is actually equivalent to $\|v_p\|_{L^2(\partial B_1)}=\|v_p\|_{L^2(\partial B_r)}$

issues.overall_effect: The alternative L^2 form of the annulus bifurcation criterion is incorrect.
issues.title: Claimed L^infty-to-L^2 equivalence drops the radius factor
issues.why_classification: A local correction of a prose consequence; no formal result depends on it.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Therein, we observe that the indicator becomes positive if and only if an eigenvalue trajectory is (i) real and (ii) traveling to the right.
On the other hand, the indicator is strictly negative for real eigenvalue curves, except at bifurcation points

issues.failure_explanation: With n_p=p^2 and kappa>0, eq:bifurc_ord gives sign(kappa')=sign(I). For p>1, eq:ind_simpl gives sign(Ibar)=-sign(I). Hence Ibar>0 iff the real trajectory travels left, the opposite of what is claimed. For the disk, Ibar=J_m(kappa_p)^2>=0, contradicting 'strictly negative', 'uniformly non-positive' and the fits Ibar ~ -|p-p*|^alpha. The cited result is also wrong: the sign relation comes from lem:bifurc_ord, not cor:bifurc.

failure_location.quote: Theory confirms this, since \cref{cor:bifurc} relates the sign of $\overline{I}$ to the sign of the derivative of a real trajectory.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Redefine Ibar = 2I/(a_m pi (p^2-1)). Flip the sign in prop:annulus:bifurc_ord accordingly, and cite lem:bifurc_ord for the sign relation.
issues.overall_effect: The claimed agreement between the numerical sign behaviour and the theory is false as defined; the plots apparently show -Ibar.
issues.title: Reported sign of the simplified indicator contradicts its definition and eq:bifurc_ord
issues.why_classification: A consistent sign convention reconciles theory and figures without changing any result.

issues.failure_explanation: The eight annulus rates average about 0.644, essentially the disk's cubic value (about 0.663), and three of them reach or exceed 2/3. Halfway between 1/2 and 2/3 would be about 0.583. By the converse of cor:bifurc_sufficient, a quadratic bifurcation requires I ~ |p-p*|^{1/2}, so the data neither show intermediate scaling nor confirm the asserted quadratic order.

failure_location.quote: we can observe an empirical scaling halfway between $-|p-p^\star|^{1/2}$ and $-|p-p^\star|^{2/3}$

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Report the rates accurately (near 2/3) and state that they are pre-asymptotic and do not confirm the 1/2 order, or refine the fits closer to p*.
issues.overall_effect: The claimed numerical confirmation of the predicted bifurcation order on the annulus is unsupported by the reported data.
issues.title: Annulus rate table does not show 'halfway' scaling or confirm the quadratic order
issues.why_classification: Correcting the interpretation of the numerical evidence leaves all formal results intact.
